title: The Invention of the Weekend
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27–40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below.

paragraphs.text: Few institutions seem as natural as the weekend. The week itself is ancient, but the idea that it should end with two consecutive days free from work is, in historical terms, extremely recent. The word 'weekend' is not recorded in English until 1879, and for decades afterwards it remained a distinctly British expression, regarded with some curiosity elsewhere.

In pre-industrial Britain, Sunday was the only official day of rest, and it was a day intended for religious observance rather than amusement. Many craftsmen, however, who were paid by the piece rather than by the hour and could therefore set their own pace, were in the habit of taking Monday off as well. The custom was known, half-jokingly, as 'keeping Saint Monday'. Monday was the day for fairs, sporting contests and, above all, drinking, and work was made up in a rush of long days at the end of the week. Benjamin Franklin, who worked in a London printing house as a young man, boasted that he won his employer's approval simply by turning up on Mondays.

Saint Monday could not survive the factory. Steam-powered machinery was expensive, and it earned nothing while standing idle; a mill in which a third of the workforce failed to appear on Monday morning could barely operate. Employers tried fines and dismissals, with limited success. What eventually worked was a bargain. From the middle of the nineteenth century, factory owners began to close at midday or two o'clock on Saturdays, on the understanding that workers would arrive punctually and sober on Monday. Reformers and church leaders supported the change, believing that a free Saturday afternoon would be spent on what they called 'rational recreation' – gardening, excursions by train, organised sport – and would leave Sunday free for church. It is no coincidence that professional football in England, with its traditional three o'clock kick-off on Saturday, dates from precisely this period.

The full two-day weekend emerged in the United States. One of the earliest known examples dates from 1908, when a cotton mill in New England granted Saturday as well as Sunday so that its Jewish workers could observe their Sabbath without having to make up the time on Sunday, which had offended some of their Christian colleagues. The decisive step, though, was taken by the car manufacturer Henry Ford, who in 1926 began closing his factories on Saturdays without reducing wages. Ford was no sentimentalist. He had concluded that people who spent all their time working had neither the opportunity nor the reason to buy the things that industry produced – including cars. Leisure, in his view, was good for business. Other manufacturers objected loudly, then gradually followed, and during the 1930s a shorter week came to be seen as a way of sharing the available work among more people at a time of mass unemployment.

Not every experiment with the calendar succeeded. In 1929, the Soviet Union abolished the seven-day week altogether. Under the new system, each worker was assigned one of five colours, and each colour had a different rest day, so that on any given day four fifths of the workforce would be at their posts and the machines need never stop. In practice, the scheme was deeply unpopular. Husbands and wives with different colours rarely shared a day off, and friends found it impossible to meet. Machinery that was never switched off, moreover, could not easily be maintained, and broke down more often. The system was modified after two years and was abandoned in 1940, when the seven-day week returned.

By the second half of the twentieth century, the five-day week had become standard across the industrialised world, and it was widely assumed that the process would continue. The economist John Maynard Keynes had predicted in 1930 that, within a hundred years, rising productivity would allow people to work as little as fifteen hours a week. Productivity did rise, much as Keynes expected. Working hours, however, stopped falling in many countries from around the 1980s, and for some professional groups they have lengthened. Why this should be so is disputed. Some economists point to the desire for ever more goods; others argue that the weakening of trade unions left employees with little power to bargain for time rather than money.

The question has recently been reopened. Trials of a four-day week, generally with no loss of pay, have been conducted in several countries, including a large one in Britain in 2022 involving around sixty companies. Most of the firms taking part reported that output had been maintained, and the great majority chose to continue after the trial ended. Such results should be read with caution, since the companies had volunteered and were therefore likely to be those best suited to the change. Even so, the history of the weekend offers one clear lesson. The length of the working week has never been fixed by nature or by economics alone. On each occasion it has been the outcome of negotiation – and what has been negotiated once can be negotiated again.

items.stem: What does the writer say about the word 'weekend' in the first paragraph?

options.A: It was borrowed from another language.
options.B: It originally referred to a religious practice.
options.C: It was for a long time used mainly in Britain.
options.D: It was in use long before 1879.

items.stem: Many craftsmen were able to 'keep Saint Monday' because

options.A: their employers approved of the custom.
options.B: their pay depended on what they produced, not on time.
options.C: Monday was an official day of rest.

items.stem: According to the writer, Saint Monday was a problem for factory owners because

options.A: their machinery made no money when it was not in use.
options.B: workers who had been drinking damaged the machinery.
options.C: church leaders criticised them for allowing it.
options.D: fines for absence were difficult to collect.

items.stem: Why did Henry Ford introduce a two-day weekend in his factories?

options.A: to allow his workers to observe a religious day
options.B: to share work among more people during a period of unemployment
options.C: because rival manufacturers had already done so
options.D: because he thought free time would lead people to buy more

groups.instruction: Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in Reading Passage 3?
groups.limit:
Write
YES if the statement agrees with the claims of the writer
NO if the statement contradicts the claims of the writer
NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this

items.text: Reformers expected workers to spend their free Saturday afternoons in worthwhile ways.
The timing of the rise of professional football in England was unconnected with the Saturday half-holiday.
Other mills in New England soon copied the 1908 arrangement.
The Soviet five-colour system made family life more difficult.
Keynes was mistaken in his expectations about productivity.
The companies in the British four-day week trial were probably typical of businesses in general.

groups.limit: Write the correct letter, A–F, next to Questions 37–40.

questions.explain:
答案是 C。原文說這個字在之後幾十年 remained a distinctly British expression，其他地方的人覺得新奇。
陷阱：D 剛好相反，原文是 not recorded in English until 1879（1879 年才第一次有紀錄）。A、B 文章都沒提。
questions.quote: for decades afterwards it remained a distinctly British expression

questions.explain:
答案是 B。工匠是 paid by the piece rather than by the hour（論件計酬），所以 could therefore set their own pace。
陷阱：C 錯在星期天才是 the only official day of rest；A 錯在雇主並不贊成，Franklin 光是星期一有來上班就得到老闆賞識。
questions.quote: who were paid by the piece rather than by the hour and could therefore set their own pace

questions.explain:
答案是 A。蒸汽機器很貴，而且 it earned nothing while standing idle（閒置時賺不到錢）。
陷阱：D 提到 fines，但原文只說罰款 with limited success（效果有限），沒說難以收取；B 的機器損壞和 C 的教會批評都沒有提到。
questions.quote: Steam-powered machinery was expensive, and it earned nothing while standing idle

questions.explain:
答案是 D。Ford 認為整天工作的人沒有機會也沒有理由買工業產品，所以 Leisure, in his view, was good for business。
陷阱：A 是 1908 年紡織廠的理由；B 是 1930 年代一般的看法，不是 Ford 的動機；C 剛好相反，其他廠商是先反對、後來才跟進。
questions.quote: people who spent all their time working had neither the opportunity nor the reason to buy the things that industry produced

questions.explain:
答案是 YES。改革者相信星期六下午會被用在 rational recreation（理性的休閒），例如園藝、搭火車出遊、有組織的運動。
同義轉換：believing... would be spent on ＝ expected... to spend；rational recreation ＝ worthwhile ways。
questions.quote: believing that a free Saturday afternoon would be spent on what they called 'rational recreation'

questions.explain:
答案是 NO。作者說 It is no coincidence（並非巧合）職業足球正好出現在這個時期，也就是兩者有關。
解題關鍵：no coincidence 表示有關聯，題目的 unconnected 與作者的看法相反。
questions.quote: It is no coincidence that professional football in England, with its traditional three o'clock kick-off on Saturday, dates from precisely this period.

questions.explain:
答案是 NOT GIVEN。文章只說這是 One of the earliest known examples，沒提其他紡織廠有沒有跟進。
陷阱：後面寫其他製造商 gradually followed，但那是跟進 Ford，不是跟進這家紡織廠。
questions.quote: One of the earliest known examples dates from 1908, when a cotton mill in New England granted Saturday as well as Sunday

questions.explain:
答案是 YES。夫妻如果被分到不同顏色，rarely shared a day off（很少同一天放假）。
同義轉換：Husbands and wives... rarely shared a day off ＝ made family life more difficult。
questions.quote: Husbands and wives with different colours rarely shared a day off

questions.explain:
答案是 NO。作者說 Productivity did rise, much as Keynes expected，他對生產力的預期是對的，沒實現的是工時下降。
陷阱：Keynes 的十五小時工作週沒有成真，容易讓人以為他整個預測都錯。題目只問 productivity 這一部分。
questions.quote: Productivity did rise, much as Keynes expected.

questions.explain:
答案是 NO。作者提醒這些公司是自願參加的，因此 likely to be those best suited to the change（很可能是最適合這種改變的公司），也就是並不具代表性。
解題關鍵：should be read with caution 之後的 since 子句說明原因，題目的 typical 與之相反。
questions.quote: the companies had volunteered and were therefore likely to be those best suited to the change

questions.explain:
答案是 C。Franklin 誇口說他只是星期一有去上班（simply by turning up on Mondays）就贏得老闆的賞識，而當時許多工匠習慣星期一不上班。
同義轉換：turning up on Mondays ＝ came to work on a day when many others did not。
questions.quote: boasted that he won his employer's approval simply by turning up on Mondays

questions.explain:
答案是 E。從不關機的機器 could not easily be maintained，所以更常故障。
同義轉換：maintained ＝ serviced；broke down more often ＝ more frequent breakdowns。
questions.quote: Machinery that was never switched off, moreover, could not easily be maintained, and broke down more often.

questions.explain:
答案是 B。有些經濟學家認為工會式微讓員工 with little power to bargain for time rather than money。
陷阱：F（拒絕接受較低工資）看似合理，但文章沒有這個說法；D 的「按工時計酬」只在講工匠時以相反的形式出現過。
questions.quote: the weakening of trade unions left employees with little power to bargain for time rather than money

questions.explain:
答案是 A。這些結果要謹慎解讀，since the companies had volunteered（因為公司是自願參加的）。
同義轉換：volunteered ＝ had chosen to take part；should be read with caution ＝ may be misleading。
questions.quote: Such results should be read with caution, since the companies had volunteered
